summary: Standards-track Telnet option that lets a client tell the server where the user's X Window display is. That way, graphical programs started on the remote machine know where to show their windows.

eli5.summary: When you run a program on a faraway computer, it needs to know which screen is yours. This is a way to hand it your screen's address.

questions: how does telnet pass the x display
what is the telnet x display location option
how does telnet pass the display variable
subtitle: A Telnet option that lets a client tell the remote host where the user's X display is.

tldr.problem: A remote Telnet host does not know the X display location of the user's Telnet client, so it cannot start other X applications on the same display.
tldr.mechanism: The X-DISPLAY-LOCATION option (code 35) lets the side that sent DO ask with a SEND subcommand, and the side that sent WILL reply with an IS subcommand holding the display string.
tldr.outcome: The display location is an NVT ASCII string in the usual DISPLAY form, sent only on request, and the memo expects hosts that transmit it to adopt this standard.

today: RFC 1096 is a Proposed Standard, and no RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Share the Display Location
sections.content:
When a user runs the Telnet client under the X window system, the remote Telnet benefits from knowing that client's X display location. The user might want to start other X applications from the remote host on the same display. This option makes that information available through Telnet connections.

It is modelled on the terminal speed option in RFC 1079, and much of its text is copied from that RFC.
sections.eli5: If you start a program far away, it needs to know which screen to show up on. This option tells it.

sections.title: Commands and Negotiation
sections.content:
The option is named X-DISPLAY-LOCATION (XDISPLOC) and has code 35. The usual WILL, WON'T, DO and DON'T commands are used. WILL and DO only obtain and grant permission. The default is WON'T and DON'T, so the location is not exchanged unless both sides agree.

After a WILL and a DO, the side that sent DO may ask for the location with IAC SB X-DISPLAY-LOCATION SEND IAC SE (SEND is code 1). Only the sender of the WILL may answer with IAC SB X-DISPLAY-LOCATION IS ... IAC SE (IS is code 0). The location may not be sent spontaneously, only in response to a request.
sections.eli5: First both sides agree they will talk about it. Then one asks, "where is your screen?" and the other answers. Nobody blurts it out unasked.

sections.title: The Location String
sections.content:
The location is an NVT ASCII string in the normal Unix DISPLAY convention: <host>:<dispnum>[.<screennum>]. No extraneous characters, such as spaces, may be included.

The RFC's example has Host2 answer with "SRI-NIC.ARPA:0.0", a command of 22 octets. It also notes that a local location such as :0 or unix:0.0 lacks a hostname, so the Telnet client must modify it appropriately before sending it on.
sections.eli5: The answer is a short line of text like an address: which computer, which display, and which screen.
